=== CALL C0490 ===
Karen: Hello. Can you hear me alright?
Andrew: Er, yeah, yeah. Loud and clear. Hi. I'm Andrew.
Karen: Karen. So we've just got to chat, have we?
Andrew: Seems that way, yeah. Three minutes. Erm, I'm not sure there's a topic, I suppose.
Karen: No. Did you finish that puzzle thing at the start?
Andrew: Er, most of it. I got stuck on the last one, the one with the shapes. I sort of ran out of time just staring at it.
Karen: Same. I hate leaving things half done. I do Wordle every morning and if I don't get it, it bothers me all day.
Andrew: What's your streak?
Karen: Two hundred and twelve.
Andrew: That's, er, that's quite serious.
Karen: It is serious. So what do you do?
Andrew: Erm, well, I'm a GIS analyst. For a water company, in Nottingham. So it's mapping, basically. Where all the pipes are, which bits flood, that sort of thing. People come to me when a dataset doesn't make sense, and I sort it out. Mostly from a back bedroom, as you can probably see.
Karen: I did wonder about the bike on the wall.
Andrew: Yeah. It lives there. Kate, my wife, wouldn't have it in the hall.
Karen: Fair enough. I'd be the same. My son leaves his stuff all over the hallway and it drives me mad.
Andrew: How old is he?
Karen: Seventeen. Doing an electrical apprenticeship. So there's tools and boots and a college bag, every single night, right where you walk in.
Andrew: Useful though, an electrician. My dad was one. He still does all his own wiring, which my mum's not keen on.
Karen: Mine's going to be doing my fuses for free. He just doesn't know it yet.
Andrew: And what about you, what's your job?
Karen: Office and transport admin at a haulage firm near Gatwick. Timesheets, MOTs, service schedules, purchase orders. Basically anything the managers don't want comes to me. Drivers are the worst. You ask for timesheets by Friday and you get them the following Wednesday, screwed up in a ball, with tea on them.
Andrew: Sounds like some of the data I get, to be honest.
Karen: Does it?
Andrew: Er, yeah. Contractors fill in a form, they put the pipe size in the wrong field, or the coordinates are in the sea off Skegness. And then I'm the one who has to sort of work out what they meant.
Karen: Yeah. And nobody thanks you for it, because when it's right nobody notices.
Andrew: That's it, really. That's exactly it.
Karen: I keep saying I want "office manager" on my contract, since that's what I actually do.
Andrew: You should, I suppose. I'm the opposite. I'd quite like to never manage anybody.
Karen: Can't blame you. Half of them can't manage themselves.
Andrew: Yeah. Er, are you local to Gatwick, then?
Karen: Crawley. Born and bred. Ten minutes from work if the A23's behaving, which it never is.
Andrew: We've got tram works in Beeston at the minute, so I sympathise. Everything's coned off for about a mile.
Karen: Is that near where—

=== CALL C0491 ===
Leanne: Hiya.
Prajakta: Hello. I'm Prajakta.
Leanne: Leanne. Sorry, can you say that again?
Prajakta: Prajakta. It's fine. People usually get it on the third go.
Leanne: Prajakta. Right. Got it.
Prajakta: So. Are you at work? You've got a fleece with a logo.
Leanne: No, I'm on lates. Start at two. I just haven't bothered getting changed.
Prajakta: What do you do?
Leanne: Shift manager. Warehouse off the M62, distribution. I run the late shift, about forty of them. Pickers, loaders, couple of team leaders.
Prajakta: Forty people. That's a lot.
Leanne: It is when half the agency don't turn up. Tuesday I had six ring in sick and three just never showed. So you're rejigging everybody, moving people off loading onto picks, and the pick rate's still got to be where it should be or I get it in the neck. D'you know what I mean.
Prajakta: Yes. I don't manage anyone. I wouldn't want to.
Leanne: Mm.
Prajakta: I'm a QC analyst. Pharmaceutical manufacturing, in Stevenage. We test the raw materials and the batches before they're released. HPLC mostly, and dissolution testing.
Leanne: No idea what them are.
Prajakta: It doesn't matter. It's checking the tablet has what it says in it, and that it dissolves properly. If it fails, it's out of specification, and then there's an investigation and a lot of paperwork.
Leanne: Sounds stressful, that.
Prajakta: It is, sometimes. If something's gone wrong I think about it at night. Even when it wasn't my mistake.
Leanne: Yeah. We've got audit in three weeks.
Prajakta: Internal or customer?
Leanne: Customer. They come round with a clipboard, check your training records, your return-to-work forms. And mine are, erm. They're not all where they should be, let's put it that way.
Prajakta: You should do them now. Not the week before.
Leanne: I know. Everyone says that.
Prajakta: Because it's right. We had an inspection last year. The people who left everything to the end were the ones who got findings.
Leanne: Bloody hell. You sound like my ops manager.
Prajakta: Sorry. I just mean it's easier.
Leanne: No, you're right. It's just boring. I'd rather be on the floor sorting stuff out than sat filling in forms.
Prajakta: I'm the opposite. I'd rather check the forms than run samples all day. That's what I want to move to, a reviewer role.
Leanne: Each to their own. Do you do long days an' all?
Prajakta: Thirty-seven and a half, plus overtime when the batches back up. Then I come home, make dinner, do my daughter's spelling. I'm shattered by nine.
Leanne: I'm not even home till gone twelve. I have me tea at like half one in the morning.
Prajakta: Tea at half one?
Leanne: Dinner, whatever. Air fryer chips usually. Dog sat there watching me.
Prajakta: That doesn't sound very healthy.
Leanne: It's not. Don't tell me mam.

=== CALL C0492 ===
Andrew: Hi. Er, can you hear me okay?
Leanne: Yeah. Hiya.
Andrew: I'm Andrew.
Leanne: Leanne.
Andrew: Right. Erm.
Leanne: Go on then, you start.
Andrew: Okay. Er, well, I'm in Beeston, near Nottingham. I do mapping for a water company. Where the pipes are, flood risk, that sort of thing.
Leanne: Is that what all the books are for?
Andrew: Er, no, those are just books. Reading's sort of my thing. And the map on the wall's old Ordnance Survey, Nottinghamshire about 1900. I like seeing what used to be there.
Leanne: Right.
Andrew: What about you?
Leanne: Warehouse. Shift manager, late shift. Normanton, off the M62.
Andrew: Normanton. I've cycled near there, actually. Along the Aire and Calder canal, out past Castleford.
Leanne: You never.
Andrew: Yeah. Leeds and back in a day, sort of a long one. There's a stretch by the river that's nicer than you'd expect.
Leanne: I walk the dog down there most mornings. Before work. That's the only bit of the day that's mine, to be honest. Once I'm in, it's agency not turning up, someone's crashed a reach truck into a racking leg, ops manager's on the phone wanting to know why the pick rate's down. Then I'm not home till gone midnight.
Andrew: That's a long day.
Leanne: It is. I'm knackered most of the time.
Andrew: What sort of dog?
Leanne: Staffy. Bella. She's chewed half the settee cushions, so she's not my favourite this week.
Andrew: We've got a cat. Moss. She's old, she's fine in the day but she wakes me at five every morning for food. Just sits on my chest.
Leanne: That's worse than the dog.
Andrew: I think it might be, yeah.
Leanne: So do you go in an office, or is it just that bedroom?
Andrew: Bit of both. Two days in Nottingham, three here. I prefer here, I suppose. It's quieter. I'm not big on people popping over to your desk.
Leanne: I'd go mad. I can't sit still. I'd rather be on the floor sorting it out myself.
Andrew: Yeah, I'd be rubbish at your job. Forty people shouting at you.
Leanne: How d'you know it's forty?
Andrew: Er, I didn't. I just guessed a big number.
Leanne: It is forty, near enough. You were spot on.
Andrew: Lucky. Erm, do you get rugby where you are? Castleford's a rugby league town, isn't it?
Leanne: Cas Tigers. Dean, that's my partner, and my dad are mad on it. I just end up shouting at the telly with them. I don't even like it that much, but I still get wound up.
Andrew: Same with my dad and Notts County. I go for him really. Sort of sit there in the cold and make the right noises.
Leanne: Is he alright, your dad?
Andrew: Er, mostly. He had a bit of a heart scare last year. He's on tablets now. Still up ladders, which he shouldn't be.
Leanne: Mine had one an' all. Doctors said it were minor, but.
Andrew: Yeah. Doesn't feel minor, does it.
Leanne: No.
Andrew: Is he behaving himself, at least?
Leanne: Is he heck. Still has a fry-up every Saturday. Mam's given up.
Andrew: Mine's started on low-fat spread and moans about it constantly. I think that's the most he'll—

=== CALL C0493 ===
Karen: Hello.
Prajakta: Hello. I'm Prajakta.
Karen: Karen. Sorry, Pra—
Prajakta: Prajakta.
Karen: Prajakta. Got it.
Prajakta: Your kitchen is very tidy. I noticed it on the photo earlier.
Karen: Thank you. It has to be, or I can't think. Yours isn't bad either.
Prajakta: It's not usually like this. I tidied before the call. When I'm stressed I reorganise the cupboards.
Karen: That's not a bad habit to have.
Prajakta: My husband thinks it is. He can't find anything afterwards.
Karen: That's his problem.
Prajakta: Yes, that's what I tell him.
Karen: So what do you do?
Prajakta: Quality control in a pharmaceutical lab. In Stevenage. I test batches before they're released.
Karen: Right. So if you get it wrong, someone gets the wrong tablets.
Prajakta: Basically. That's why I check everything twice. Some people in my lab don't. They write things in the notebook half done and then I have to chase them.
Karen: Oh, I know that one. I do admin for a haulage firm. Drivers' timesheets, vehicle schedules, purchase orders. If one form's wrong, a lorry's off the road, or we fail a compliance check, and guess whose desk that lands on. Not the bloke who couldn't be bothered to fill in a box.
Prajakta: Yes. And nobody remembers that you fixed it.
Karen: No. They just remember if it went wrong.
Prajakta: I had a team leader before who did that. Blamed me for someone else's mistake in front of everyone. I still think about it.
Karen: Did you say anything?
Prajakta: I did. It didn't help. He moved on, but nobody ever said sorry.
Karen: They never do. My lot take it for granted. I've been there eleven years and my title's still "administrator". I basically run the place.
Prajakta: You should ask for it in writing.
Karen: I have. Twice.
Prajakta: Then ask a third time. With a list of what you actually do.
Karen: That's not a bad idea, actually. I've got it all on a spreadsheet anyway.
Prajakta: Of course you have.
Karen: Of course I have. Is that your little one's bag on the chair?
Prajakta: Yes, Ira. She's seven. The school sends emails at nine o'clock at night saying tomorrow is non-uniform day, bring a pound. Every time.
Karen: Nothing changes. Mine's seventeen and I had that for ten years. It doesn't get easier, you just stop caring about the pound.
Prajakta: I don't think I will stop caring. I worry about everything with her.
Karen: You do. Even at seventeen. He's on an electrical apprenticeship, and I still worry he'll electrocute himself.
Prajakta: That's a reasonable worry.
Karen: I thought so. Nobody else does.
Prajakta: Do you have help? Family nearby?
Karen: My mum, she's in Crawley. She's seventy-eight now, so it's more me helping her these days. Yours?
Prajakta: In Pune. India. My mother-in-law comes for a few months, but my parents are there. It's far.
Karen: That must be hard.
Prajakta: It is. I don't really—

=== CALL C0494 ===
Andrew: Hi. Er, hello.
Prajakta: Hello. I'm Prajakta.
Andrew: Andrew. Sorry, Prajakta, is that right?
Prajakta: Yes. First time. That's rare.
Andrew: I was concentrating.
Prajakta: So what do you do?
Andrew: Erm, mapping. GIS, for a water company. Pipe networks, flood risk, that sort of thing. I'm in Beeston, just outside Nottingham.
Prajakta: Is that why there's a map behind you?
Andrew: Sort of. That's an old Ordnance Survey one, about 1900. The old ones are more of a hobby, really. You can see where the pits were, and the railways that aren't there any more.
Prajakta: And the clothes on the radiator?
Andrew: Er. That's a cycling jersey. I went out this morning and got rained on. I should've moved it before the call, I suppose.
Prajakta: I noticed it on the photo earlier. It's fine.
Andrew: It's honest, at least. What about you?
Prajakta: QC analyst. Pharmaceutical manufacturing, in Stevenage. I test the batches before they're released.
Andrew: So, checking things are what they say they are.
Prajakta: Yes. And checking other people haven't made mistakes.
Andrew: That's quite a lot of my job as well, actually. Contractors send in survey data and half of it's wrong. Pipe diameters in the depth column, or the coordinates put a manhole in the middle of the Trent. And I'm the one who's meant to work out what they actually meant.
Prajakta: Do you tell them?
Andrew: Er, mostly I just fix it. Then I send a polite email.
Prajakta: I tell them. Directly. People think I'm sharp because of it, but if I don't say anything, it happens again next week.
Andrew: You're probably right. I should be more like that.
Prajakta: Probably.
Andrew: Erm. Are those spice tins on the shelf? The steel ones?
Prajakta: Yes. Do you cook?
Andrew: Most nights, yeah. Dal, a chickpea curry, a few things from a Middle Eastern cookbook I'm working through. Nothing fancy.
Prajakta: Where do you buy your spices?
Andrew: Er, the supermarket, mostly.
Prajakta: That's the problem. They sit on the shelf for a year and they taste of nothing. Go to an Indian grocer. Buy whole spices, small packets, and toast them yourself. I drive to Hitchin for mine.
Andrew: Right. There's a few in Nottingham. I'll try that.
Prajakta: You'll notice the difference. Straight away.
Andrew: I'll report back. Well, I won't, I suppose. But I'll know.
Prajakta: Yes. You'll know.
Andrew: Do you get back to India much?
Prajakta: Every year or so. Pune. Usually December, for three weeks. I hate the flight, and leaving is worse. My father had a heart problem two years ago, so each time I go I'm thinking, is this the last time I see him like this.
Andrew: Yeah. My dad had a scare last year. It's not the same, he's only up the road, but I get it. You sort of watch them differently after.
Prajakta: Yes. That's exactly it. You watch them.
Andrew: Is he alright now?
Prajakta: He's fine. He walks every morning. My mother phones me if he doesn't.
Andrew: That's good. Mine's back up ladders, which is less good.
Prajakta: Then tell him. Directly.
Andrew: Ha. Yeah, maybe I'll start with him.
Prajakta: Where would you go? If you could travel anywhere.
Andrew: Er, Iceland, I think. Or Japan. Somewhere I could—

Karen: Oh, I know that one. I do admin for a haulage firm. Drivers' timesheets, vehicle schedules, purchase orders. If one form's wrong, a lorry's off the road, or we fail a compliance check, and guess whose desk that lands on. Not the bloke who couldn't be bothered to fill in a box.
Prajakta: Yes. And nobody remembers that you fixed it.
Karen: No. They just remember if it went wrong.
Prajakta: I had a team leader before who did that. Blamed me for someone else's mistake in front of everyone. I still think about it.
Karen: Did you say anything?
Prajakta: I did. It didn't help. He moved on, but nobody ever said sorry.
Karen: They never do. My lot take it for granted. I've been there eleven years and my title's still "administrator". I basically run the place.
Prajakta: You should ask for it in writing.
Karen: I have. Twice.
Prajakta: Then ask a third time. With a list of what you actually do.
Karen: That's not a bad idea, actually. I've got it all on a spreadsheet anyway.
Prajakta: Of course you have.
Karen: Of course I have. Is that your little one's bag on the chair?
Prajakta: Yes, Ira. She's seven. The school sends emails at nine o'clock at night saying tomorrow is non-uniform day, bring a pound. Every time.
Karen: Nothing changes. Mine's seventeen and I had that for ten years. It doesn't get easier, you just stop caring about the pound.
Prajakta: I don't think I will stop caring. I worry about everything with her.
Karen: You do. Even at seventeen. He's on an electrical apprenticeship, and I still worry he'll electrocute himself.
Prajakta: That's a reasonable worry.
Karen: I thought so. Nobody else does.
Prajakta: Do you have help? Family nearby?
Karen: My mum, she's in Crawley. She's seventy-eight now, so it's more me helping her these days. Yours?
Prajakta: In Pune. India. My mother-in-law comes for a few months, but my parents are there. It's far.
Karen: That must be hard.
Prajakta: It is. I don't really—
calls.C0494:
Andrew: Hi. Er, hello.
Prajakta: Hello. I'm Prajakta.
Andrew: Andrew. Sorry, Prajakta, is that right?
Prajakta: Yes. First time. That's rare.
Andrew: I was concentrating.
Prajakta: So what do you do?
Andrew: Erm, mapping. GIS, for a water company. Pipe networks, flood risk, that sort of thing. I'm in Beeston, just outside Nottingham.
Prajakta: Is that why there's a map behind you?
Andrew: Sort of. That's an old Ordnance Survey one, about 1900. The old ones are more of a hobby, really. You can see where the pits were, and the railways that aren't there any more.
Prajakta: And the clothes on the radiator?
Andrew: Er. That's a cycling jersey. I went out this morning and got rained on. I should've moved it before the call, I suppose.
Prajakta: I noticed it on the photo earlier. It's fine.
Andrew: It's honest, at least. What about you?
Prajakta: QC analyst. Pharmaceutical manufacturing, in Stevenage. I test the batches before they're released.
Andrew: So, checking things are what they say they are.
Prajakta: Yes. And checking other people haven't made mistakes.
Andrew: That's quite a lot of my job as well, actually. Contractors send in survey data and half of it's wrong. Pipe diameters in the depth column, or the coordinates put a manhole in the middle of the Trent. And I'm the one who's meant to work out what they actually meant.
Prajakta: Do you tell them?
Andrew: Er, mostly I just fix it. Then I send a polite email.
Prajakta: I tell them. Directly. People think I'm sharp because of it, but if I don't say anything, it happens again next week.
Andrew: You're probably right. I should be more like that.
Prajakta: Probably.
Andrew: Erm. Are those spice tins on the shelf? The steel ones?
Prajakta: Yes. Do you cook?
Andrew: Most nights, yeah. Dal, a chickpea curry, a few things from a Middle Eastern cookbook I'm working through. Nothing fancy.
Prajakta: Where do you buy your spices?
Andrew: Er, the supermarket, mostly.
Prajakta: That's the problem. They sit on the shelf for a year and they taste of nothing. Go to an Indian grocer. Buy whole spices, small packets, and toast them yourself. I drive to Hitchin for mine.
Andrew: Right. There's a few in Nottingham. I'll try that.
Prajakta: You'll notice the difference. Straight away.
Andrew: I'll report back. Well, I won't, I suppose. But I'll know.
Prajakta: Yes. You'll know.
Andrew: Do you get back to India much?
Prajakta: Every year or so. Pune. Usually December, for three weeks. I hate the flight, and leaving is worse. My father had a heart problem two years ago, so each time I go I'm thinking, is this the last time I see him like this.
Andrew: Yeah. My dad had a scare last year. It's not the same, he's only up the road, but I get it. You sort of watch them differently after.
Prajakta: Yes. That's exactly it. You watch them.
Andrew: Is he alright now?
Prajakta: He's fine. He walks every morning. My mother phones me if he doesn't.
Andrew: That's good. Mine's back up ladders, which is less good.
Prajakta: Then tell him. Directly.
Andrew: Ha. Yeah, maybe I'll start with him.
Prajakta: Where would you go? If you could travel anywhere.
Andrew: Er, Iceland, I think. Or Japan. Somewhere I could—
calls.C0495:
Karen: Hello.
Leanne: Hiya.
Karen: We're wearing the same thing.
Leanne: Ha. Navy fleece, grey T-shirt. Work uniform?
Karen: Not officially. It just is.
Leanne: Same. I'm Leanne.
Karen: Karen. Are you off to work?
Leanne: Lates, yeah. Warehouse. I'm a shift manager off the M62, distribution. You?
Karen: Admin for a haulage firm near Gatwick. Timesheets, MOTs, purchase orders. I'll probably end up dealing with drivers who've been to your sort of place.
Leanne: Probably. Sorry about them in advance.
Karen: It's fine. They're all the same. You ask for one simple thing and it comes back a week late with a coffee ring on it.
Leanne: Try agency staff. Half of them don't turn up, and the half that do don't know what a scanner is. And I've got a customer audit in three weeks, and me return-to-work forms are, erm. Let's say they're in a pile.
Karen: How big a pile?
Leanne: Big enough.
Karen: Do one a day. Start tonight. Put them in date order and tick them off on a sheet so you can see it going down.
Leanne: You're the second person today who's told me that.
Karen: Then it's probably right.
Leanne: That's what she said an' all.
Karen: Well. Great minds.
Leanne: It's not that I can't do it. I'd just rather be on the floor sorting stuff than sat in the office with a pen. D'you know what I mean.
Karen: I do. But the auditor doesn't care where you'd rather be.
Leanne: No. Fair.
Karen: Is that a dog lead behind you?
Leanne: Bella. Staffy. She's eaten the settee cushions this week, so she's in my bad books. Grey velvet an' all, from Dunelm.
Karen: That's expensive chewing.
Leanne: Tell me about it. What are you doing for your holidays this year, anything?
Karen: Tenerife. Same place as last year. I know the hotel, I know the pool, I know which sunbeds get the shade.
Leanne: I've done Tenerife. Lanzarote, Turkey twice, Majorca. I like knowing what I'm getting. Dean wants to try somewhere new and I'm like, why?
Karen: Exactly. Why pay to be disappointed?
Leanne: I hate the flying, though. I have a couple of drinks at the airport, just to calm meself down.
Karen: I'm ten minutes from Gatwick, so I'm there and through security before I've had time to worry.
Leanne: Lucky. I have to go to Leeds Bradford or Manchester. It's—

C0490.line_text: Mine's going to be doing my fuses for free. He just doesn't know it yet.
C0490.what: A teenage boy in a hoodie walks across the kitchen behind Karen, opens the fridge on the right, takes out a carton of milk, and walks back out of frame without looking at the camera.
